People exchange their views in a conversation.
Pexels · 9811867
The limits of consensus
Consensus can legitimise collective action, but unanimity alone proves little. Agreement deserves authority when participation is
substantively fair and decisions remain open to revision; these conditions matter more than the appearance of complete alignment.
Fair participation requires scrutiny of how alternatives are framed. A neighbourhood committee may vote unanimously for a venue
after consulting only residents who can attend evening meetings. The result appears orderly, yet excludes relevant experience. Such
omissions bear on legitimacy even when formal procedures are followed.
Revisability provides a second safeguard against premature closure. The committee could circumscribe its decision-making
authority, record objections and review the venue after a trial event. This approach enables action while preserving a route for
overlooked needs to influence the outcome.
Legitimate consensus therefore combines inclusive deliberation with accountable revision. It holds decisiveness and openness in
tension, allowing people to act together without pretending that differences have disappeared. A collective voice earns authority by
remaining answerable to its constituent voices.
BUILD YOUR OWN · Qualify the claim that consensus legitimises action. Examine inclusive participation, then revisability, using a
connected example. Synthesize the conditions of legitimate agreement. Follow the main idea through two supported points. The
conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
Why does the writer distinguish unanimity from legitimate agreement? (Model: Unanimity can result from deference or exclusion, so
legitimacy depends on the conditions of participation and the continuing possibility of disagreement.)
